figures.caption: Figure 2: Orientation selectivity across training paradigms. A. We show RSS, ORS, and bandwidth (HWHM) against relative depth, one L-tier backbone per paradigm. All show an inverted-U RSS profile but diverge in where it decays: DINOv2/DINOv3 sustain it deepest, AIMv2 collapses earliest, and MAE keeps rising to the final layer. The shaded band marks V1-like bandwidths (15◦–40◦), and hollow circles mark blocks with fewer than 20 significant units. B. The same metrics within the contrastive family isolate data and loss as the only variables.

Figure 3: We plot RSS vs. relative depth, for each family, across tiers. Tiers overlay almost exactly within every family except AIMv2, the only one that fixes depth and scales width alone, whose RSS curve changes substantially with scale.

Figure 4: Orientation selectivity over OpenCLIP ViT-H/14’s training trajectory. Left: we plot mean OSI, ORS, and circular variance against training epoch (log scale, 0 = untrained), one line per layer (dark = shallow, light = deep), against the random-init floor (dashed). Right: we plot the same metrics at the final checkpoint (last 10 epochs, averaged) against the untrained floor, across layer depth; shading marks where training raises (green) or lowers (pink) a layer’s value. Early-to-mid layers recruit more orientation-selective units than they start with; deep layers lose selectivity with training.

Table 1: Per-task validation performance of each frozen, L-tier backbone under the minimal linear/1×1conv read-out described above (task, dataset, and metric definitions in Table 3). Bold green marks the best backbone per task and bold terracotta the worst; retrieval is a tie for best between two backbones. Metrics are on different scales across columns (accuracy, mAP, mIoU, . . . ) and are not directly comparable across tasks; see Fig. 6 for the pooled, min–max normalized comparison.

Table 2: Models used in cross-model and cross-scale experiments, grouped by scale tier. Cells report parameter count / number of transformer blocks. AIMv2 fixes depth at 24 across all tiers and scales width instead, so its Huge/Giant entries are not block-matched to the other families in their row.
Table 3: Benchmarked tasks, datasets, and primary metrics. Tracking (MOT16) is registered but excluded: the public mirror was unreachable at data-collection time, leaving 9 of 10 tasks scored.

Figure 6: We plot mean min–max normalized performance S(b) (Eq. 11) for the six L-tier frozen backbones, pooled across benchmark tasks (0 = worst, 1 = best backbone per task). DINOv3 generalizes best (0.958), followed by DINOv2 (0.670) and SigLIP2 (0.521); MAE (0.405) and DeiT3 (0.393) are similarly mid-low, and AIMv2 generalizes worst (0.138).

Figure 7: Protocol schematic. Top: the frozen backbone is probed once with the RSA battery at every block, giving an a-priori RSS-vs-block curve, no fine-tuning required. Bottom: for each block k, the same backbone is adapted with LoRA on blocks [k :] and fine-tuned across the 9 Taskonomy-style tasks (5 seeds each), giving an empirical pooled-performance-vs-k curve. RSS’s peak, measured without any fine-tuning, coincides with the pooled-performance peak, making RSS an a-priori predictor of where to unfreeze.
